title: How 4 companies are taking action to tackle extreme heat at work
gist: Extreme heat already exposes over 2.4 billion workers (70%+ of the global workforce) and is projected by the ILO to cost $2.4 trillion a year in lost productivity by 2030, yet a BCG survey for the World Economic Forum finds that although 80% of companies see it as a business threat, about 50% have not started a systematic assessment and only 28% have piloted interventions. The piece profiles Mahindra Group, JINGDONG Logistics, Turner Construction and Bayer as early movers, citing hard results such as Bayer's 20% cut in North American heat incidents and JINGDONG's RMB 100 million driver protection plan.

themes.theme: Scale of heat exposure and productivity cost

insights.claim: According to 2024 International Labour Organization estimates, more than 2.4 billion workers, over 70% of the global working population, are exposed to excessive heat at work, and 2026 is on track to be the hottest year on record.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Heat exposure is a mainstream labour-supply risk rather than a niche one, so it belongs in productivity and margin assumptions for labour-intensive sectors.

insights.claim: The ILO links excessive workplace heat to almost 19,000 worker deaths and nearly 23 million injuries a year.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Heat-related injury volumes point to rising workers' compensation, liability and regulatory exposure for employers with outdoor workforces.
insights.quote: The same ILO report links excessive heat to almost 19,000 worker deaths and nearly 23 million injuries a year.

insights.claim: Extreme heat is projected to cause $2.4 trillion in annual productivity losses by 2030, according to the International Labour Organization.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: A macro-scale productivity drag that falls hardest on hot-climate, labour-intensive economies. Watch for it in output and GDP revisions in South Asia, the Middle East and similar regions.

insights.claim: Construction, agriculture, logistics and mining workers face the most heat exposure because they work outdoors, but office workers are also affected by heat on their commute and by heat-disrupted sleep at home.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Construction, agriculture, logistics and mining margins are the most exposed to heat-adaptation costs and lost hours, and the productivity hit also reaches white-collar workers indirectly.
insights.locator: Workers in sectors characterized by outdoor environments

themes.theme: Corporate execution gap on heat resilience

insights.claim: In a Boston Consulting Group survey for the World Economic Forum, 80% of companies recognize extreme heat as a business threat, but about 50% across all major geographies and sectors have not begun a systematic assessment of their workforce and value chain, and only 28% have piloted interventions.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Most corporates have not priced in physical heat risk to their labour, which leaves room for negative surprises in operations-heavy names and a large untapped market for adaptation services.
insights.locator: Yet while 80% of companies surveyed by Boston Consulting Group

insights.claim: Companies are slow to act on extreme heat for three practical reasons: it is hard to quantify the financial impact, ownership across functions is unclear, and they face technical or resource constraints.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Tools that quantify heat-related losses (wearables, risk analytics, cost-per-claim data) address the main blocker to corporate spending on heat, so they are the likely first place adaptation budgets go.
insights.locator: These include difficulty quantifying financial impacts

insights.claim: The World Economic Forum/BCG report proposes a seven-step Workforce Heat Resilience Roadmap that runs from risk diagnostics across value chains to context-specific solution design, then capability-building to test, scale and embed resilience into daily operations.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: A disclosure yardstick: ask exposed companies whether they have done value-chain heat diagnostics and pilots, or are still at the 'awareness' stage.
insights.locator: Looking ahead in an ever warming world

insights.claim: Mahindra Group, with 320,000+ workers in more than 100 countries, divides its workforce into three heat-risk profiles: outdoor workers (farmers, security guards, delivery workers) with the highest exposure, indoor workers in non-air-conditioned or enclosed spaces, and mobile field workers in construction or logistics whose exposure varies as they move between settings.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Segmenting by exposure profile is a practical template for scoring heat risk in a labour-heavy portfolio company, rather than treating the workforce as one uniform risk.
insights.locator: Mahindra, India – identifying worker risk profiles

insights.claim: Mahindra's heat response combines governance, heat action plans and audits with physical site upgrades (reflective coatings, rooftop insulation, better ventilation), nature-based pilots (tree canopy cover, water features), shift times moved around peak temperatures, mobile hydration stations and protective equipment.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Heat adaptation creates retrofit demand for cool-roof coatings, insulation and ventilation at industrial sites in hot markets such as India.
insights.locator: Mahindra, India – identifying worker risk profiles

themes.theme: JINGDONG Logistics: paying for heat in last-mile delivery

insights.claim: JINGDONG Logistics has invested RMB 100 million (about $15 million) in a summer protection plan for delivery drivers. The plan includes a heat subsidy paid from April to October that is set dynamically by regional temperature, and it suspends deliveries during extreme weather while keeping safeguards for driver income.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Temperature-indexed pay and weather-related delivery stoppages build climate costs directly into last-mile unit economics. Model seasonal cost-per-parcel inflation and service interruptions for delivery platforms in hot regions.
insights.locator: JINGDONG Logistics, China – protecting frontline workers

insights.claim: At delivery stations and sorting centres, JINGDONG Logistics stocks ice popsicles and cold drinks and gives drivers and couriers 'cooling packs' with cooling sleeves, sun hats, rehydration and first-aid supplies, backed by health and safety training on recognizing heat stress early and triggering emergency response for heat stroke.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Low-cost, frontline-level measures are the first line of heat protection in logistics, which means recurring operating costs rather than one-off capex.
insights.locator: JINGDONG Logistics, China – protecting frontline workers

themes.theme: Turner Construction: measuring heat stress with wearables

insights.claim: In a pilot study by Turner Construction and the nonprofit La Isla Network, among construction workers who spent at least a quarter of their day outside climate-controlled settings, two-fifths had core body temperatures above 38°C and many arrived at work already dehydrated.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Measured physiological strain on US construction sites points to hidden productivity losses and safety liabilities that contractors will increasingly need to price into bids and schedules.
insights.quote: two-fifths experienced core body temperatures greater than 38°C
insights.locator: Turner Construction, US – interventions that work in context

insights.claim: Turner Construction is using wearables to test which heat interventions work, including pop-up shade tents, air-conditioned cooling stations, lunch tents and electrolyte popsicles, while moving work schedules away from peak heat.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Wearable-based heat monitoring is becoming an evidence tool in construction and is an emerging demand niche for occupational-safety wearables. Shifting hours away from peak heat also has consequences for project timelines.
insights.locator: Turner Construction, US – interventions that work in context

themes.theme: Bayer: measured ROI and supply-chain heat protection

insights.claim: Bayer's standardized heat-risk management across more than 300 active sites worldwide has reduced heat-related incidents in North America by 20%, saving an estimated $3,000 in avoided medical and lost-time costs per prevented claim.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: One of the few hard ROI figures for workplace heat programmes. It gives a per-claim benchmark for sizing avoided costs and supports the business case that the survey says companies struggle to make.
insights.locator: Bayer, Global – extending protection to downstream value chains

insights.claim: Bayer is one of the first multinationals to extend heat-resilience protocols beyond its own staff to downstream value-chain workers, specifically smallholder farmers in India, in order to protect farmer health and productivity and keep agricultural supply continuous.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Heat risk in agri-input value chains reaches customer and supplier productivity. Companies that protect downstream farmers may gain stickier demand and more secure supply as heat intensifies.
